questions.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $10x$ is the derivative of the quantity in the square root. So we make a substitution

$$
u=5{x}^{2}-4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =10x\,⟹\,\text{d}u=10x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 10x\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,10x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=5{x}^{2}-4$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 10x\sqrt{5{x}^{2}-4}\,\text{d}x=\frac{2(5{x}^{2}-4)^{3/2}}{3}+C.
$$

We note that $5{x}^{4}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the radical. So we make a substitution

$$
u=1+{x}^{5}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{1/2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =2{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =2\sqrt{u}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{5}$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-1).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-1.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}-1)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-1)^{3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{u}^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-1)^{4}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=1+x-{x}^{4}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1-4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=(1-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1-4{x}^{3}}{1+x-{x}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{1+x-{x}^{4}}\cdot (1-4{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|1+x-{x}^{4}|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{6}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{7}}{7}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{28}{u}^{7}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{28}{(1+2{x}^{2})}^{7}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Using Natural Logarithms
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $u=x^3+1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 3x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u= x^2 \, \textrm d x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}+1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{3}+1}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|{x}^{3}+1|+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u = 1 - x^3.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3x^2 \quad \Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac{1}{3} \textrm d u= x^2 \, \textrm d x,
$$

and we can solve the resulting integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(2\sqrt{u})+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{1-{x}^{3}}+C\end{aligned}
$$
